quote: and that Jane would perceive the sarcasm
content: The name is Keysar’s. His 1994 paper is titled "The Illusory Transparency of Intention" and reports the sarcasm studies the essay describes (Keysar 1994, "The Illusory Transparency of Intention," Cognitive Psychology 26(2):165–208); the essay cites Keysar and Barr and uses their term for their result. Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec’s effect shares the name and is a different finding, which is a fact about the psychological literature rather than a conflation by the essay. Two research groups converging on one label for two overestimates of how legible one’s own mind is to others is a point in favor of the underlying phenomenon; the June/Jane slip is a slip.

quote: Additional subjects who overheard the explanation showed no such bias, expecting listeners to understand in only 56% of cases.
content: The design controls the base rate, which is why the comparison is informative. Speakers and overhearers were shown the same message and asked the same question; the only difference was that the speaker knew what he had meant. That difference produced an eleven-point overestimate against the overhearers’ five-point underestimate, and it is the difference, not either absolute number, that measures the illusion. The general effect — that knowing something makes it feel more inferable from the evidence than it is — is the curse of knowledge, which replicates in markets, in children and in adults across dozens of studies (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber 1989; Birch & Bloom 2007).
